title: Severe hyponatremia in a patient with schizophrenia associated with prolonged consciousness disturbance
case_prompt:
A 30-year-old Japanese man with a 7-year history of schizophrenia and longstanding water-drinking behavior (≈10 L/day) presented with 6 days of progressive nausea. Two days before admission he developed mild disorientation and speech disturbance.  
On transfer to the regional emergency hospital his Glasgow Coma Scale was E4V1M5. Physical examination showed no signs of volume overload or depletion and no focal neurologic deficits. Chest radiography was unremarkable.  
His outpatient regimen included over 10 oral psychotropic agents, all of which were discontinued on admission.  
Laboratory tests revealed: serum sodium 96 mEq/L, potassium 1.9 mEq/L, plasma osmolality 195 mOsm/kg; urine sodium 53 mEq/L, urine osmolality 332 mOsm/kg; urine-specific gravity 1.011; normal adrenal and thyroid studies; fractional excretion of sodium 0.45 %; negative free water clearance.  
An echocardiogram showed normal left ventricular size and systolic function. Renin–aldosterone activity was not elevated. Extracellular fluid volume was judged to be normal.  
He was fluid-restricted (≤500 mL/day) and received hypertonic (3%) saline and isotonic extracellular-like fluid, with serum sodium monitored every 4 h. Twelve hours after initiation, sodium had risen by 12 mEq/L and hypertonic saline was stopped. On day 3, serum sodium was 121 mEq/L and mental status improved to GCS E4V4M6.  
On hospital day 2 (after transfer), consciousness again deteriorated to GCS E4V1M4 without focal weakness. Brain MRI on day 3 showed bilateral high-intensity signals in the ventral posterolateral nucleus on T2-weighted images.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Salt-losing hyponatremia was excluded — “No increase was observed in the urinary Na excretion rate, eliminating the possibility of Na-losing hyponatremia.”  
2. Hypovolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia was excluded — “we estimated that there were neither major increases nor decreases in the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume.”  
3. SIADH was considered as the primary cause of dilutional hyponatremia — “we speculated that this was likely to have been caused by drug-induced SIADH, as the patient had been taking a large number of oral antipsychotic agents…”  
4. Psychotic polydipsia was viewed as an exacerbating factor — “we noted that the patient had psychotic polydipsia due to the psychiatric disorder, and we speculated that this also had an exacerbating effect on the hyponatremia.”  
5. Hypokalemic nephropathy–related concentrating defect was considered but deemed less likely — “the possible involvement of a hypokalemic nephropathy-related urine concentration disturbance should be considered, but the patient's polyuria was almost restored within the first 3 days before the normalization of his serum K concentration, suggesting that the massive water intake would be more likely…”  
6. Osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS) was suspected for the persistent consciousness disturbance — “we suspected a condition resembling extrapontine myelinolysis (EPM) … hyperintensity was also observed on T2-weighted imaging in the ventral lateral thalamic nucleus, which was consistent with an image finding of EPM.”  
7. ODS alone was questioned because MRI findings persisted despite clinical improvement — “in many cases abnormal findings on MRI scans disappeared after EPM/CPM symptoms disappeared, which is inconsistent with the present case.”  
8. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (malignant hyperthermia syndrome) was considered after antipsychotic discontinuation — “we considered neuroleptic malignant syndrome as a differential diagnosis … fever, a consciousness disturbance, muscular stiffness … occurred 4 days after the discontinuation of antipsychotic intake.”
